findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
findings.body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from the incoming request context. Once the REST handler returns its successful unified-storage response, the server cancels that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy operation as well (the 10-second timeout does not detach it from its parent). Consequently legacy creates, updates, deletes, and collection deletes can be aborted simply because the response was sent, defeating the intended asynchronous mirror write. Create a detached context (while preserving needed values/logging) before applying the legacy-write timeout.

findings.title: Independent goroutines allow legacy mutations to be applied out of order
findings.body: Every successful unified write starts an independent legacy-write goroutine with no ordering or per-object serialization. For example, a client can create an object and immediately update or delete it: unified storage observes that order, but the legacy update/delete can run before the legacy create, or the create can complete after a delete. This leaves the legacy store missing mutations or containing stale/deleted objects. The asynchronous replication path needs an ordered queue/worker (at least keyed by resource) or another mechanism that preserves mutation ordering.

findings.title: Legacy update re-evaluates UpdatedObjectInfo instead of mirroring the unified update result
findings.body: After Storage.Update has invoked objInfo to produce and persist the unified object, the asynchronous Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo and invokes it again against legacy state. UpdatedObjectInfo callbacks are not guaranteed to be idempotent: they may depend on the old object, apply generated values, or perform request-scoped work. Thus the two stores can receive different updates, and the callback is unexpectedly evaluated twice. The prior implementation computed the update once and used wrappers to supply the resulting object to both writes; mode 3 needs to preserve that behavior while making the legacy write asynchronous.

findings.title: Several mode 3 metrics are recorded against the wrong operation or labels
findings.body: The Create and Update unified-storage error paths call recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), and the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166). In addition, successful Delete records the resource name as the kind label (line 106). These paths make storage/legacy latency and error metrics inaccurate and can create a high-cardinality metric label from arbitrary object names, preventing reliable monitoring of replication failures.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify completion of asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The tests return immediately after the unified call and never synchronize with the spawned legacy goroutine or assert mock expectations. They can therefore pass when the legacy write is canceled, never runs, or fails, which misses the core mode-3 requirement. Add deterministic signaling/waiting in the mock and assertions that the legacy operation is invoked after successful unified writes; integration checks that immediately read the legacy API should similarly poll or otherwise wait for eventual replication.
